newsitem.title: GERMANY: Schering eyes new record after strong profits.
newsitem.headline: Schering eyes new record after strong profits.

text.p: German drugs group Schering AG reported Monday that its nine-month profits jumped 66 percent, proving business was back on track and could set a record for 1996 just months after a string of serious problems.

Schering Chief Executive Giuseppe Vita, clearly pleased that results topped forecasts, said net profit climbed to 286 million marks ($190 million) while sales climbed 12 percent to 3.85 billion ($2.56 billion).
"Who would have dreamed a year ago that Schering would already be able to present such a pleasing nine-month profit today? -- the numbers top even our own expectations," Vita told a news conference.

Schering Chief Financial Officer Klaus Pohle told a news conference 1996 profits will show a 34 percent rise, from 249 million marks ($166 million) a year ago, when currency turmoil seriously dented results.
Full-year sales at the world's largest maker of oral contraceptives are expected to top 5.2 billion marks ($3.46 billion).
Shareholders will profit from the recovery as the board plans to raise this year's dividend payout to two marks per share from 1.55 marks paid out for 1995, Pohle said.

But Schering also warned against an overly optimistic outlook, saying profits would have risen only 34 percent on an adjusted basis since the group took a huge writedown last year after it pulled its new x-ray drug Isovist 280 off the market.
For 1997, Pohl sees profits growing in single digit percentage point rates, with sales totalling 5.9 billion marks ($3.9 billion).

Analysts, welcoming the nine-month data, said Schering's outlook was slightly disappointing. "I think the group was a bit conservative for next year," said Markus Rausch, at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Frankfurt.
In the first nine months, volume sales, rising 12 percent, and stabler currency relations were instrumental to growth with multiple-sclerosis drug Betaferon contributing strong sales.
"We generate our profits largely abroad," Pohle said, adding that sales in Latin America, the United States, Schering's largest single market, and southern Europe led the way.

Betaferon sales climbed by 36 percent to nearly 400 million marks ($266 million), leaving Schering confident it can still reach its full-year sales target of 535 million marks ($356 million), trimmed back from 600 million marks ($399 million) after the launch in Europe proved difficult.
In the United States, where the drug is called Betaseron and has enjoyed several years of unrivalled sales, Schering said it was feeling the launch of rival Biogen's Avonex product.
But Vita was optimistic that patients who switched to Avonex complaining of flu-like side effects with Betaseron will soon return, as Avonex's dosage is weaker.
